      - heading "Color roles" [level=1]
      - text: "There are 26 standard color roles organized into six groups: primary, secondary, tertiary, error, surface, and outline"
      - navigation "page content":
        - text: On this page
        - list:
          - listitem:
            - link "What are color roles?"
          - listitem:
            - link "General concepts"
          - listitem:
            - link "Accent color roles"
          - listitem:
            - link "Primary"
          - listitem:
            - link "Secondary"
          - listitem:
            - link "Tertiary"
          - listitem:
            - link "Error"
          - listitem:
            - link "Surface"
          - listitem:
            - link "Outline"
          - listitem:
            - link "Add-on color roles"
      - tabpanel:
        - region:
          - button "copy link to What are color roles? section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "What are color roles?" [level=2]
          - paragraph: Color roles are like the "numbers" in a paint-by-number canvas. They're the connective tissue between elements of the UI and what color goes where.
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - strong: Color roles are mapped to Material Components
              - text: You'll use these color roles whether you're using the static baseline scheme or dynamic color. If your product contains custom components, they'll need to be properly mapped to this set of color roles.
            - listitem:
              - strong: Color roles ensure accessibility
              - text: The color system is built on accessible color pairings. These color pairs provide an accessible minimum 3:1 contrast.
            - listitem:
              - strong: Color roles are tokenized
              - text: Roles are implemented in design and code through tokens. A design token represents a small, reusable design decision that’s part of a design system's visual style.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure "Diagram of all Material color roles, including optional add-on roles for surface colors and fixed accent colors":
            - img "Example color swatches for all 45 color roles including Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Error, Surfaces, Inverse roles, Scrim and Shadow roles."
            - paragraph: Diagram of all Material color roles, including optional add-on roles for surface colors and fixed accent colors
        - region:
          - button "copy link to General concepts section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "General concepts" [level=2]
          - paragraph: "Here are helpful-to-know words you'll see in the names of color roles:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - strong: Surface
              - text: – A role used for backgrounds and large, low-emphasis areas of the screen.
            - listitem:
              - strong: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary
              - text: – Accent color roles used to emphasize or de-emphasize foreground elements.
            - listitem:
              - strong: Container
              - text: – Roles used as a fill color for foreground elements like buttons. They should not be used for text or icons.
            - listitem:
              - strong: "On"
              - text: – Roles starting with this term indicate a color for text or icons
              - emphasis: on top
              - text: of its paired parent color. For example,
              - strong: on primary
              - text: is used for text and icons against the
              - strong: primary
              - text: fill color.
            - listitem:
              - strong: Variant
              - text: – Roles ending with this term offer a lower emphasis alternative to its non-variant pair. For example,
              - strong: outline variant
              - text: is a less emphasized version of the
              - strong: outline
              - text: color.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Pairing and layering colors" [level=3]

    <span class="tooltip-text ">

      " tabindex="0" role="tooltip" id="tooltip-838">

    </span>

            <a class="tooltip-link-content " tabindex="0" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank" href="/m3/pages/static/baseline">More on baseline color</a>
          </span>
  </span></span></span></span> or <span class="tooltip-link" tabindex="0">
    <span class="tooltip-text ">
    <span class="tooltip-label" aria-describedby="tooltip-381">dynamic color<span class="tooltip-parent tooltip-container
      " tabindex="0" role="tooltip" id="tooltip-381">
    <span class="tooltip-content">

    </span>
      <span class="tooltip-action" tabindex="0">
            <a class="tooltip-link-content " tabindex="0" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank" href="/m3/pages/dynamic/choosing-a-source">More on dynamic color</a>
          </span>
  </span></span></span></span>. If your product contains custom components, they'll need to be properly mapped to this set of color roles.</li><li><strong>Color roles ensure accessibility</strong><br>The color system is built on <span class="tooltip-link" tabindex="0">
    <span class="tooltip-text ">
    <span class="tooltip-label" aria-describedby="tooltip-87">accessible color pairings<span class="tooltip-parent tooltip-container
      " tabindex="0" role="tooltip" id="tooltip-87">
    <span class="tooltip-content">

    </span>
      <span class="tooltip-action" tabindex="0">

          </span>
  </span></span></span></span>. These color pairs provide an accessible minimum 3:1 contrast.</li><li><strong>Color roles are tokenized</strong><br>Roles are implemented in design and code through tokens. A <span class="tooltip-link" tabindex="0">

            - listitem:

            - link "panes":

          - paragraph: "When dividing a screen into layout panes, consider the breakpoint:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: "Compact and medium breakpoints: A single pane works best"
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: "Expanded and large breakpoints: Two panes are recommended"
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: "Extra-large breakpoints: Consider using three panes"
          - figure "Compact and medium breakpoints should use a single pane, while larger breakpoints can use two":
            - img "A compact and medium window have a single pane. A larger window has 2 panes."
            - paragraph: Compact and medium breakpoints should use a single pane, while larger breakpoints can use two
        - region:

          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: At medium breakpoints, two panes are useful when they contain low-density content with clear actions.
          - paragraph: Don’t use two panes in medium layouts with high information density, as it can reduce usability.

          - paragraph: UI elements that are small on compact screens can grow as breakpoints increase. Panes can also expand to rearrange elements and make better use of space.

          - paragraph: Resizing can highlight imagery and improve text readability. This type of adaptation affects the scale of content and the relationship between objects on screen.           - paragraph: Across all breakpoints, adjust margins and type styles to keep text between 40–60 characters per line.

          - paragraph: A UI and its components can reflow or reposition to make use of additional space on expanded screens and in resized panes.       - tabpanel:
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Hierarchy section": link

          - heading "Hierarchy" [level=2]
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: When navigation is easy, users understand where they are in your app and what’s important. To emphasize which information is important, multiple visual and textual cues like color, shape, text, and motion add clarity.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Types of feedback" [level=3]
          - paragraph: Visual feedback (such as labels, colors, and icons) and touch feedback show users what is available in the UI.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Navigation" [level=3]
          - paragraph: Navigation can have clear task flows with minimal steps, easy-to-locate controls and clear labeling. Focus control, or the ability to control keyboard and reading focus, can be implemented for frequently used tasks.
          - paragraph:
            - text: Every added button, image, and line of text increases the complexity of a UI.
            - strong: "Y"
            - strong: "ou can simplify how your UI is understood by using:"
          - list:
            - listitem: Clearly visible elements
            - listitem: Sufficient contrast and size
            - listitem: A clear hierarchy of importance
            - listitem: Key information that is discernable at a glance
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Levels of importance" [level=3]
          - paragraph:
            - strong: "To convey an item’s relative level of importance:"
          - list:
            - listitem: Place important actions at the top or bottom of the screen (reachable with shortcuts)
            - listitem: Place related items of a similar hierarchy next to each other
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Visual hierarchy" [level=3]
          - paragraph: To enable the screen reader to read out content in the intended order, it’s important for designers to collaborate with developers – both for writing out the HTML in the correct order, and understanding how screen readers will interpret designs.
          - paragraph: While CSS determines the layout and appearance of a page, screen readers rely on the top-down structure of HTML on any platform (mobile or web). This structure creates a map for the screen reader to follow when reading the content.
          - figure "An example of how content hierarchy in a screen can be identified in a logical reading order to optimize for the ways assistive tech, such as screen readers, may interpret information":
            - img "Example of a mobile app using 4 content cards in a 2 by 2 grid. They reading order is top left, to top right, then bottom left, then bottom right."
            - paragraph: An example of how content hierarchy in a screen can be identified in a logical reading order to optimize for the ways assistive tech, such as screen readers, may interpret information
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Web landmarks and headings section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Web landmarks and headings" [level=2]
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph:
            - strong: Define content and UI layout to improve navigation and comprehension.
          - paragraph: Assistive technologies (AT) rely on clear, delineated structures to process page information, navigating primarily through the use of headings and landmarks. Many assistive technologies, such as screen readers, translate a design into a linear experience, which means that many users interact with content in hierarchical, predetermined order. Therefore, thinking through structural decisions in advance can improve the accessibility of a product.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph:
            - strong: For web only
            - text: ": Landmarks and headings help assistive-technology users orient themselves to a web page and allow for easy navigation and traversal across large sections of a document or page."
          - paragraph:
            - text: By
            - strong: classifying and labeling sections of a page
            - text: ", structural information that is conveyed visually through layout design can also be represented in code."
          - figure "Example of a page diagram mapping the areas for a UI in order to consider the relative landmarks and headings":
            - img "Diagram of a website, showing different regions and their associated landmarks and headings."
            - paragraph: Example of a page diagram mapping the areas for a UI in order to consider the relative landmarks and headings
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Identifying landmarks and headings" [level=3]
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "1. Define landmarks" [level=4]:
            - strong: 1. Define landmarks
          - paragraph: Landmarks are large blocks of content that establish the high-level structure of your layout. They're a set of Accessible Rich Internet Applications (ARIA) roles that provide easy access to, and important meaning for, common content areas of a web page.
          - paragraph:
            - text: "There are eight landmark roles:"
            - strong: navigation, search, main, banner, complementary, contentinfo, region, and form
            - text: .
          - paragraph: "The eight landmark roles in the W3C ARIA guidelines include:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - strong: Navigation
              - text: ": Contains lists of navigation links (there can be multiple, in which case you should differentiate in label)"
            - listitem:
              - strong: Search
              - text: ": A search field"
            - listitem:
              - strong: Main
              - text: ": The main content area as defined by UX. There should be only one."
            - listitem:
              - strong: Banner
              - text: ": Typically the header; content repeated from page to page, often contains navigation and toolbars. There should be only one."
            - listitem:
              - strong: Complementary
              - text: ": A sidebar or aside to main content that can stand alone without the main content"
            - listitem:
              - strong: Contentinfo
              - text: ": Typically the footer; contains information describing the site and its content (for example, copyright). There should be only one."
            - listitem:
              - strong: Region
              - text: ": Content regions are important content blocks. They can be nested inside the “main” landmark. Regions should be labeled with names that make the purpose of that region clear."
            - listitem:
              - strong: Form
              - text: ": Takes and stores user info."
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Add accessibility labels" [level=4]:
            - strong: Add accessibility labels
          - paragraph:
            - text: Add
            - strong: clear and specific labels
            - text: to any landmark roles that appear multiple times (regions or navigation typically). This will help users differentiate information.
          - paragraph:
            - text: Labels should be added to
            - strong: all regions
            - text: ", as well as any landmark where a label will enhance meaning. For example, explaining the contents or purpose of a sidebar."
          - paragraph:
            - strong: Don't repeat the landmark role within a label
            - text: .
          - figure "This layout has two areas assigned the navigation role. Each landmark should get a unique label to help users tell the difference between elements.":
            - img "Diagram labeling two regions with a navigation role with the labels primary and pagination"
            - text: This layout has two areas assigned the navigation role. Each landmark should get a unique label to help users tell the difference between elements.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "2. Define headings" [level=4]:
            - strong: 2. Define headings
          - paragraph: Assistive technology users often navigate web pages with the help of headings. They create a clear hierarchy to help users navigate and take action.
          - list:
            - listitem: Identify headings based on content hierarchy, rather than visual styling
            - listitem: Headings should not skip a level, for example, don't go from H2 to H4 without using an H3
            - listitem: Map content on your pages to headings (H1–H6) in sequential order based on the hierarchy of your content
            - listitem: A single H1 for the page title is recommended
          - figure "Example of headings marked up in code":
            - img "Diagram labeling different headings"
            - text: Example of headings marked up in code
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Consider hierarchy in addition to style" [level=4]:
            - strong: Consider hierarchy in addition to style
          - paragraph:
            - strong: Ensure that headings correspond with meaningful titles
            - text: . If they don't, consider changing the titles in the UI to benefit the experience of all users or adding a label for assistive tech.
          - paragraph: Heading levels are informed by the layout's information architecture—the structural hierarchy that’s applied to a set of items. The page’s visual styling does not need to match the heading levels in terms of prominence and visual hierarchy.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Target sizes section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Target sizes" [level=2]
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: Material Design’s target guidelines can help users who aren’t able to see the screen, or who have difficulty with small touch targets, to tap elements in your app.
          - figure:
            - img "Target guidelines on buttons for easy accessibility."
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Touch and pointer target sizes" [level=3]
          - paragraph: Touch targets are the parts of the screen that respond to user input, extending beyond the visual bounds of an element. For example, an icon may appear to be 24 x 24dp, but the padding surrounding it comprises the full 48 x 48dp touch target.
          - paragraph: For most platforms, consider making touch targets at least 48 x 48dp. A touch target this size results in a physical size of about 9mm, regardless of screen size. The recommended target size for touchscreen elements is 7-10mm. It may be appropriate to use larger touch targets to accommodate a larger spectrum of users.
          - paragraph: "Note: iOS recommends 44 x 44dp targets."
          - 'figure "Icons: 24dp Star icon: 40dp Touch target on both: 48dp"':
            - img "A row of four 24dp icons and one 40dp icon"
            - paragraph: "Icons: 24dp"
            - paragraph: "Star icon: 40dp"
            - paragraph: "Touch target on both: 48dp"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Pointer targets" [level=3]
          - paragraph: Pointer targets are similar to touch targets, but are implemented by motion-tracking pointer devices such as a mouse or a stylus.
          - paragraph: Consider making pointer targets minimums 44 x 44dp.
          - 'figure "Recommended target size for pointers: 44dp"':
            - img "A row of four icon buttons in the bottom app bar."
            - text: "Recommended target size for pointers: 44dp"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Target spacing" [level=3]
          - paragraph: In most cases, targets separated by 8dp of space or more promote balanced information density and usability.
          - 'figure "Two groups of icons showing their overall spacing and the spacing between each other Touch target size: 48dp Padding: 8dp"':
            - img "Three icons in a row with 48dp touch target size and three icons in a row with 8dp padding between icons."
            - paragraph: Two groups of icons showing their overall spacing and the spacing between each other
            - paragraph: "Touch target size: 48dp"
            - paragraph: "Padding: 8dp"

class="text-chunk ng-star-inserted"><h4 id="isPasted"><strong>1. Define landmarks </strong></h4><p>Landmarks are large blocks of content that establish the high-level structure of your layout. They're a set of Accessible Rich Internet Applications (ARIA) roles that provide easy access to, and important meaning for, common content areas of a web page. </p><p>There are eight landmark roles: <strong>navigation, search, main, banner, complementary, contentinfo, region, and form</strong>. </p><p>The eight landmark roles in the W3C ARIA guidelines include:</p><ol><li><strong>Navigation</strong>: Contains lists of navigation links (there can be multiple, in which case you should differentiate in label)</li><li><strong>Search</strong>: A search field</li><li><strong>Main</strong>: The main content area as defined by UX. There should be only one.</li><li><strong>Banner</strong>: Typically the header; content repeated from page to page, often contains navigation and toolbars. There should be only one.</li><li><strong>Complementary</strong>: A sidebar or aside to main content that can stand alone without the main content</li><li><strong>Contentinfo</strong>: Typically the footer; contains information describing the site and its content (for example,  copyright). There should be only one.</li><li><strong>Region</strong>: Content regions are important content blocks. They can be nested inside the “main” landmark. Regions should be labeled with names that make the purpose of that region clear. </li><li><strong>Form</strong>: Takes and stores user info.</li></ol></div><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----></div><!----><!----><!----></div><!----><!----><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" role="region" class="block snug ng-star-inserted" id="ed2aad37-be51-4b35-905f-7f24f17bc8aa"><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="copy-button-container focusable"><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" mioripple="" class="google-symbols copy-button notranslate" aria-label="copy link to this section" role="button" tabindex="0">link<div class="ripple"></div></div><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="copy-button-background"></div><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="tooltip"><span _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="deactivated">Copy link</span><span _ngcontent-roq-c26="" aria-live="polite" class="activated">Link copied</span></div></div><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="scroll-target"></div><!----><!----><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="chunk ng-star-inserted" style="grid-column: span 1;"><!----><div _ngcontent-roq-c26="" class="text-chunk ng-star-inserted"><h4 id="isPasted"><strong>Add accessibility labels </strong></h4><p>Add <strong>clear and specific labels</strong> to any landmark roles that appear multiple times (regions or navigation typically).           - paragraph: Enabled buttons need a 3:1 contrast ratio with the background to meet accessibility best practices.
          - paragraph: This is measured from the container for elevated, filled, and tonal button styles, and the label text for outlined and text button styles.

          - paragraph: Avoid excessive text wrapping or truncation by choosing concise strings.
          - paragraph: On Android, button labels should be kept concise enough to fit within two lines after the text size is increased to 200%. If a button label exceeds this limit and gets truncated, provide an alternative way to access the full content in a single tap.
          - figure "exclamation Caution Avoid excessive text wrapping or truncation by choosing concise strings":

      - text: Design tokens are the building blocks of all UI elements. The same tokens are used in designs, tools, and code.
      - navigation "article tabs":

          - tab "Overview"

      - tabpanel:

          - button "copy link to Download Material baseline tokens section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Download Material baseline tokens" [level=2]
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph:
            - text: Material Design’s baseline theme includes design tokens and default values.
            - link "Download the theme":
              - /url: http://github.com/material-foundation/material-tokens
            - text: as a Design System Package (DSP) to customize, collaborate on, and use in your own designs and product code.
            - link "Learn about the DSP JSON format":
              - /url: https://github.com/AdobeXD/design-system-package-dsp
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Use tokens in Figma section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Use tokens in Figma" [level=2]
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph:
            - text: To begin, install the
            - link "Material Theme Builder":
              - /url: https://goo.gle/material-theme-builder-figma
            - text: Figma plugin from the community page.
          - paragraph
          - heading "Generate tokens" [level=3]
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - text: "Open Figma and navigate to:"
              - strong: Plugins
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Material Theme Builder
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Open Plugin
            - listitem:
              - text: Select
              - strong: Get started
              - text: ", this will create"
              - strong: material-theme
              - text: with baseline values by default. Color and text styles will begin populating the right hand design panel. When your tokens are fully generated, your artboard will contain tonal palettes for light and dark color schemes, as well as a default type scale.
            - listitem:
              - text: Your tokens are now represented as
              - link "Figma styles":
                - /url: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360039238753-Styles-in-Figma
              - text: that can be used throughout your designs
          - paragraph
          - heading "Update token values" [level=3]
          - heading "Using the Material Theme Builder Figma plugin (updates colors only)" [level=4]
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - text: "Open Figma and navigate to:"
              - strong: Plugins
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Material Theme Builder
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Open Plugin
            - listitem: Choose the colors. Updated color and text styles will begin populating the right hand design panel.
            - listitem:
              - text: Your updated tokens are now represented as
              - link "Figma styles":
                - /url: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360039238753-Styles-in-Figma
              - text: that can be used throughout your designs
          - paragraph
          - heading "Using Figma styles" [level=4]
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - text: "In Figma, navigate to the file in which the tokenized style is defined. Shortcut: right click the style in the right hand sidebar and select"
              - strong: Go to style definition.
            - listitem:
              - text: In the right hand sidebar, hover over the style you want to update and
              - strong: select the adjust icon when it appears
              - text: . Or, right click the style in the style picker and select
              - strong: Edit style
              - text: .
            - listitem:
              - text: Make your changes to the token name, description, properties, etc. using the
              - strong: Edit style panel
              - text: . Close the panel when finished.
          - paragraph
          - heading "Use tokens in product mock-ups" [level=3]
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - text: Instead of manually setting the color or typography for elements in a layout, apply the
              - link "Figma styles":
                - /url: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360039238753-Styles-in-Figma
              - text: representing your design tokens. This helps ensure that developers will correctly understand and apply your design choices.
          - paragraph
          - heading "Use tokens with the Material Design Kit" [level=3]
          - list:
            - listitem: Duplicate the Material Design Kit in Figma
            - listitem:
              - text: Navigate to
              - strong: Plugins
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Material Theme Builder
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Open plugin
            - listitem:
              - text: With components selected,
              - strong: select swap
              - text: . This will swap the baseline Material token style values with your own generated token style values.
          - paragraph
          - heading "Export tokens" [level=3]
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - text: "Open Figma and navigate to:"
              - strong: Plugins
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Material Theme Builder
              - text: ">"
              - strong: Open Plugin
            - listitem:
              - text: Navigate to the
              - strong: Export tab
              - text: . Select the format you want to export for (Android, Jetpack Compose)
            - listitem:
              - text: Name your .zip file and select
              - strong: Save
          - paragraph: Your tokens are ready to share!

class="text-chunk ng-star-inserted"><p dir="ltr">To begin, install the <a href="https://goo.gle/material-theme-builder-figma" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Material Theme Builder</a> Figma plugin from the community page.</p><p><br></p><h3 dir="ltr">Generate tokens</h3><ol><li>Open Figma and navigate to: <strong>Plugins</strong> > <strong>Material Theme Builder</strong> > <strong>Open Plugin</strong></li><li>Select <strong>Get started</strong>, this will create <strong>material-theme</strong> with baseline values by default. Color and text styles will begin populating the right hand design panel. When your tokens are fully generated, your artboard will contain tonal palettes for light and dark color schemes, as well as a default type scale.</li><li>Your tokens are now represented as <a href="https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360039238753-Styles-in-Figma" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Figma styles</a> that can be used throughout your designs</li></ol><p><br></p><h3 dir="ltr">Update token values</h3><h4 dir="ltr">Using the Material Theme Builder Figma plugin (updates colors only)</h4><ol><li>Open Figma and navigate to: <strong>Plugins</strong> > <strong>Material Theme Builder</strong> > <strong>Open Plugin</strong></li><li>Choose the colors. Updated color and text styles will begin populating the right hand design panel.</li><li>Your updated tokens are now represented as <a href="https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360039238753-Styles-in-Figma" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Figma styles</a> that can be used throughout your designs</li></ol><p><br></p><h4 dir="ltr">Using Figma styles</h4><ol><li>In Figma, navigate to the file in which the tokenized style is defined. Shortcut: right click the style in the right hand sidebar and select <strong>Go to style definition.</strong></li><li>In the right hand sidebar, hover over the style you want to update and <strong>select the adjust icon when it appears</strong>. Or, right click the style in the style picker and select <strong>Edit style</strong>.</li><li>Make your changes to the token name, description, properties, etc. using the <strong>Edit style panel</strong>. Close the panel when finished.</li></ol><p><br></p><h3 dir="ltr">Use tokens in product mock-ups</h3><ol><li>Instead of manually setting the color or typography for elements in a layout, apply the <a href="https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360039238753-Styles-in-Figma" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Figma styles</a> representing your design tokens. This helps ensure that developers will correctly understand and apply your design choices.</li></ol><p><br></p><h3 dir="ltr">Use tokens with the Material Design Kit</h3><ol><li>Duplicate the Material Design Kit in Figma</li><li>Navigate to <strong>Plugins</strong> > <strong>Material Theme Builder</strong> > <strong>Open plugin</strong></li><li>With components selected, <strong>select swap</strong>. This will swap the baseline Material token style values with your own generated token style values.</li></ol><p><br></p><h3 dir="ltr">Export tokens</h3><ol><li>Open Figma and navigate to: <strong>Plugins</strong> > <strong>Material Theme Builder</strong> > <strong>Open Plugin</strong></li><li>Navigate to the <strong>Export tab</strong>. Select the format you want to export for (Android, Jetpack Compose)</li><li>Name your .zip file and select <strong>Save</strong></li></ol><p dir="ltr">Your tokens are ready to share!</p></div><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----></div><!----><!----><!----></div><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----><!----></article><!----><!----><!----></mio-carbon-component></div><!----></div></main><nav           - heading "What’s Material 3 Expressive?" [level=2]
          - paragraph: Today, people increasingly see their devices not as tools, but as extensions of themselves. Expressive interfaces have an emotional impact, fostering connection by evoking a feeling or mood through visual design and interaction. Material 3 Expressive is an evolution of the Material 3 design system. It’s a set of new features, updated components, and design tactics for creating emotionally impactful UX.
          - paragraph:
            - link "We’ve learned":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/blog/testing-material-3?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25
            - text: that makers are looking for ways to improve their user experiences by creating better hierarchy, making the interface more useful, and establishing improved, more personal styles that connect emotionally with their users.
          - paragraph: And to be clear — M3 Expressive isn’t a new version of the system. We’re not deprecating M3, and this isn’t “M4.”
        - region:
          - button "copy link to The power of expressive design section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "The power of expressive design" [level=2]
          - paragraph: "M3 Expressive is our most researched update to the design system since its launch in 2014. Extensive user research — 46 studies with more than 18,000 participants — has helped ensure that this evolution isn’t just about aesthetics, but about truly enhancing your users’ experience. Our top research takeaways include:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Expressive designs are preferred by people of all ages.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Expressive designs consistently score higher on user attributes like playfulness, energy, creativity, and friendliness.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Users are more likely to switch to products that use M3 Expressive components and techniques.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Expressive designs are easier to use, with participants spotting key UI elements up to four times faster in expressive screens.
          - paragraph:
            - link "Learn more about the Expressive research over on design.google.":
              - /url: https://design.google/library/expressive-material-design-google-research?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25
          - paragraph

          - heading "Motion-physics system" [level=4]
          - paragraph: A new system using motion springs makes interactions and transitions feel more alive, fluid, and natural.
          - paragraph: Spatial springs mirror the physics of how objects actually move, making animations clear and predictable. Effects springs create seamless transitions for color and opacity changes.
          - paragraph:
            - link "Learn more about motion":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/overview?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25

        - region:

          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Visually emphasized typography" [level=4]
          - paragraph: New type styles for variable and static fonts can be used to express a range of emotional states, automatically adjust variables for readability, and support bold editorial layouts.
          - paragraph: Emphasized typography reinforces the information hierarchy and draws attention to important actions, like “begin recording,” or information, like unread messages.
          - paragraph:
            - link "Learn more about typography":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/styles/typography/overview?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25

          - heading "Expanded shape library" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Use the new set of 35 shapes to add decorative detail for elements like image crops and avatars.
          - paragraph: A built-in shape-morph animation allows smooth transitions from one shape to another. This can be dynamic, or as simple as a square changing to a circle.
          - paragraph:
            - link "Learn more about shape":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/styles/shape/overview?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25

          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Vibrant color schemes" [level=4]
          - paragraph: An expanded range of colors can be used to sharpen hierarchy and clarify key actions. Rich visual styles support personalization and dynamic colors.

          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Expressive tactics" [level=3]
          - paragraph: As Google products started using the new expressive features, we quickly established a set of design tactics to help guide the viewer’s attention to the most important elements of the screen. Each of these tactics represents one axis along which you can make your components, layouts, and products more expressive. While these tactics work for us, the beauty of this update is that makers have more flexibility with M3 than ever before, so we encourage you to play around with these elements and see what works for you.
          - heading "1. Use a variety of shapes" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Shape can be a powerful communication tool in your interface. At the base level of visual design, the shapes of components, containers, and content set the tone for a user at first glance. Combining shapes and corner radii can create visual tension or cohesion and direct users’ focus in your app. Use a combination of classic and abstract shapes to create unique silhouettes or groupings. Use the shape library and the new corner-radii options to mix round and square shapes for tension and visual contrast.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure "exclamation Caution Smaller shapes can result in essential actions looking less important.":
            - text: exclamation Caution
            - paragraph: Smaller shapes can result in essential actions looking less important.
          - figure "check Do Break from the surrounding shape style to draw attention to a particular element.":
            - text: check Do
            - paragraph: Break from the surrounding shape style to draw attention to a particular element.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "2. Apply rich and nuanced colors" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Material’s dynamic color system already offers a range of colors for primary, secondary, and tertiary elements and surfaces. Mixing these colors for key components or visual elements can help emphasize the main takeaway of a screen. Create visual hierarchy with surface tones. Use contrast between primary, secondary, and tertiary color roles to prioritize actions and simplify navigation.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure "exclamation Caution Without contrast, elements can blend together.":
            - text: exclamation Caution
            - paragraph: Without contrast, elements can blend together.
          - figure "check Do Use contrast to emphasize the main takeaway or element.":
            - text: check Do
            - paragraph: Use contrast to emphasize the main takeaway or element.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "3. Guide attention with typography" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Use emphasized text styles to draw attention to important UI elements, like headlines and actions. Create editorial-like moments in your app by emphasizing typography. Heavier weights, larger sizes, color, and spacing can direct attention and make key information more engaging. Using additional type styles from the Material type scale can help create appropriate hierarchy within and between blocks of content.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure "Expressive typography can enhance hierarchy and add personality.":
            - paragraph: Expressive typography can enhance hierarchy and add personality.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "4. Contain content for emphasis" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Organize content into logical groupings or containers. Give the most important content, tasks, or actions visual prominence through ample space and the brightest surface mapping. Consider using size, spacing, rhythm, similarity, or other grouping principles to make important elements more distinct.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure "exclamation Caution Ungrouped information can blend together.":
            - text: exclamation Caution
            - paragraph: Ungrouped information can blend together.
          - figure "check Do Group similar content into informative groupings.":
            - text: check Do
            - paragraph: Group similar content into informative groupings.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "5. Add fluid and natural motion" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Make interactions feel alive and spirited through shape morph or surface effects. Apply the expressive motion springs or custom micro animations.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link

            - paragraph: Examples of expressive motion in a range of apps and devices.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "6. Leverage component flexibility" [level=4]
          - paragraph: UI should adapt to the user context. Shift components or controls depending on the environment to make completing tasks easier. Adapt content to foldable and large screens through custom tweaks or by applying canonical layouts.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link

        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "7. Combine tactics to create hero moments" [level=4]
          - paragraph: Hero moments use multiple expressive tactics to break from predictable or uniformly applied design ideas. They’re meant to make a stand-alone statement or frame essential information in a fresh, editorial way. Hero moments can be a focusing mechanism. Invest your time in making the most critical interactions sing; these moments are the heart of your product!
          - paragraph: Hero moments are brief, delightful, surprising, and unexpected. Stick to one or two hero moments in your product; too many moments can be overwhelming or distracting.
          - paragraph: "To identify your hero moment, ask yourself:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: Is this interaction emotionally impactful?
                - text: Consider whether a design choice can highlight an emotional reaction or emphasize familiarity.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: Is this a key interaction in your product?
                - text: Think about whether a detail or flow can be emphasized for clarity. Guide the user’s attention by making an important button dominant, or emphasizing key information.

Expressive interfaces have an emotional impact, fostering connection by evoking a feeling or mood through visual design and interaction. Material 3 Expressive is an evolution of the Material 3 design system. It’s a set of new features, updated components, and design tactics for creating emotionally impactful UX.</p><p><a href="https://m3.material.io/blog/testing-material-3?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25" target="_self">We’ve learned</a> that makers are looking for ways to improve their user experiences by creating better hierarchy, making the interface more useful, and establishing improved, more personal styles that connect emotionally with their users.</p><p>And to be clear — M3 Expressive isn’t a new version of the system.           - paragraph:
            - text: Material Design has an exciting new preview release —
            - link "Material 3 Expressive":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/blog/building-with-m3-expressive?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO25
            - text: ". In this latest version 1.4.0-alpha14 of Material 3, you get access to a new theming system: motion!"
          - paragraph: Previously, Material motion was defined through non-customizable easing and duration values. Today, we’re introducing a new, customizable motion scheme using motion physics defined through a set of motion properties. These can be customized or overridden as needed, giving you more control than ever over how motion works and feels in your product.
          - paragraph: Read on to learn how the new motion physics scheme works, how existing APIs have changed, and how to get started.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link

        - region:
          - button "copy link to Why Material motion? section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Why Material motion?" [level=2]
          - paragraph: "As a product developer, you know that motion can significantly enhance the user experience. But achieving consistent motion across a complex app can be challenging. The new Material motion system solves this with:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: "Centralized control:"
                - text: Define your motion theme once, and all Material Components and even your own custom components will inherit it, creating a unified and polished experience, eliminating scattered animation specs.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: "Simplified theming:"
                - text: Stop fussing with individual duration or easing values. Choose from predefined schemes or create your own, using physics-based spring animations for a natural and engaging feel.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: "Adaptive animations:"
                - text: Ensure that movement feels fast in the context of the device and adjusts based on user input since animations are not based on predefined time sets.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Getting setup section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Getting setup" [level=2]
          - paragraph: "First, make sure you’re using the latest version of Compose Material 3:"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link androidx.compose.material3:material3:1.4.0-alpha11
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: If you do nothing more than update the Compose dependency, your apps will benefit from applying the standard motion scheme to all your uses of Material Components. But if you do want that extra bit of control, you can customize your scheme to suit your app.
          - paragraph:
            - emphasis: "Note: When 1.4.0 goes to stable, the Material Expressive APIs will move to the next alpha (1.5.0-alphaX), and will no longer be available in 1.4.0. The APIs will go stable in the 1.5.0 release."
        - region:

          - paragraph:
            - text: "The physics system has two preset motion schemes:"
            - strong: Expressive
            - text: and
            - strong: Standard
            - text: . The scheme you choose will define how your product feels. While most motion in a product should use the same scheme, advanced customizations allow you to swap the scheme to emphasize key moments.
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: Expressive
                - text: is Material’s recommended motion scheme, and should be used for most situations, particularly hero moments and key interactions.
            - listitem:
              - paragraph:
                - strong: Standard,
                - text: with its small amount of bounce, feels more functional and should be used for utilitarian products.

            - strong: Speed tokens work across devices.
            - text: For example, the
            - strong: Spatial “fast”
            - text: token will always be faster than
            - strong: “default”
            - text: or
            - strong: “slow,”
            - text: but the exact values of each token will differ depending on whether the device is a wearable, phone, or tablet. This ensures the movement feels fast in the context of the device. This also applies when using spring tokens in a custom motion scheme.

        - region:

          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: Notice that the Expressive and Standard schemes are presets of opinionated motion values. This makes it easier to swap schemes without changing the underlying property names.

          - heading "Why use motion springs?" [level=2]
          - paragraph: If you look at the predefined specifications on the motion schemes, you may notice that springs are used for the backing specifications. Why is this? Spring animations appear more natural by allowing for the ability to interrupt and retarget the animation when required.
          - paragraph: "For example, consider the difference between using tween and springs:"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure "Tween interruptions.":
            - button "Pause Video": pause
            - paragraph: Tween interruptions.
          - figure "Spring interruptions.":
            - button "Pause Video": pause
            - paragraph: Spring interruptions.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: When interrupted and retargeted to a new destination, the spring animation uses its current velocity to perform a more seamless transition between the two states than tween.
          - paragraph:
            - text: It’s also beneficial to use springs to ensure your animations easily
            - strong: adapt to different screen sizes
            - text: ", as the tokens will always be slow or fast in the context of the device since it is not time that is specified but rather damping and stiffness. For more details on the benefits of springs, check out the"
            - link "documentation":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/customize?_gl=1*9ewdxh*_ga*MzI1NjMyOTExLjE3NjI0MTE3NDU.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3NzQzNDgyNDgkbzE3OCRnMCR0MTc3NDM0ODM1MCRqNjAkbDAkaDA.#spring?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=motion&utm_campaign=IO25
            - text: .

          - heading "Customizing your motion scheme" [level=2]
          - paragraph: The real power of the new system lies in its flexibility. You can tailor the motion scheme to reflect your app’s brand or to underscore an important interaction.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Choosing between Standard and Expressive schemes" [level=3]
          - paragraph: "Most developers won’t want to change much in terms of motion theming, but there are two out-of-the-box options for you to choose from: Standard or Expressive. Choosing MaterialExpressiveTheme at the top level will default to the Expressive motion scheme."
          - paragraph: Make this choice once for your application at the theme level, and any Material Components with movement built in will use the selected spec from the theme.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: "Copy link @Composable fun YourCustomTheme(){ MaterialExpressiveTheme( motionScheme = MotionScheme.expressive(), // or MotionScheme.standard() ) { } }"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: With the expressive() scheme your apps take on the Material-recommended motion scheme, whereas with the standard(), the motion is, well, pretty standard — there is a minimal amount of bounce, even as both use springs under the hood.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Creating your own Motion scheme" [level=3]
          - paragraph: For more fine-grained control, you can create your own MotionScheme object and return a different AnimationSpec for each property.
          - paragraph: In the code snippet below, we create a whole new playfulMotionScheme that by default adds a lot of bounce to components. This demonstrates how you can customize your MotionScheme.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: "Copy link @ExperimentalMaterial3ExpressiveApi fun playfulMotionScheme(): MotionScheme = object : MotionScheme { override fun <T> defaultEffectsSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<T> { return spring( dampingRatio = Spring.DampingRatioNoBouncy, stiffness = 1600f ) } override fun <T> defaultSpatialSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<T> { return spring(dampingRatio = 0.6f, stiffness = 700f) } override fun <T> fastEffectsSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<T> { return spring(dampingRatio = Spring.DampingRatioNoBouncy, stiffness = 3800f) } override fun <T> fastSpatialSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<T> { return spring(dampingRatio = 0.6f, stiffness = 1400f) } override fun <T> slowEffectsSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<T> { return spring(dampingRatio = Spring.DampingRatioNoBouncy, stiffness = 800f) } override fun <T> slowSpatialSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<T> { return spring(dampingRatio = 0.6f, stiffness = 300f) } } // To use the scheme: In your top level composable @Composable fun MyCustomTheme( //... other theme properties content: @Composable () -> Unit ) { MaterialExpressiveTheme( //.... other theme properties motionScheme = playfulMotionScheme(), content = { content() } ) }"
        - region:

          - heading "Custom component animations" [level=2]
          - paragraph: To maintain consistency with other Material Components, ensure your custom components adopt the recommended motion changes and use the motion specs available through MaterialTheme.motionScheme.
          - paragraph: "For example, the following code uses tween() calls to animate the size and color of a text component when pressing and releasing its container:"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: "Copy link val interactionSource = remember { MutableInteractionSource() } val isPressed by interactionSource.collectIsPressedAsState() val scale by animateFloatAsState( targetValue = if (isPressed) 8f else 1f, animationSpec = tween(1000), label = \"scale\" ) val color by animateColorAsState( targetValue = if (isPressed) Color.Green else Color.Red, animationSpec = tween(1000), label = \"color\" ) Box( modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize().clickable( interactionSource = interactionSource, indication = null ) {} ) { Text( text = \"Hello\", modifier = Modifier.graphicsLayer { scaleX = scale scaleY = scale transformOrigin = TransformOrigin.Center } .align(Alignment.Center), style = LocalTextStyle.current.copy(color = color, textMotion = TextMotion.Animated) ) }"
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph: Since scale represents a Spatial motion and color falls under Effects motion, we can leverage the motion scheme for consistent application. This approach aligns your component’s motion to the overall app experience and allows it to adapt automatically when switching between Standard and Expressive schemes/themes.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: "Copy link val interactionSource = remember { MutableInteractionSource() } val isPressed by interactionSource.collectIsPressedAsState() val scale by animateFloatAsState( targetValue = if (isPressed) 8f else 1f, animationSpec = MaterialTheme.motionScheme.defaultSpatialSpec<Float>(), label = \"scale\" ) val color by animateColorAsState( targetValue = if (isPressed) Color.Green else Color.Red, animationSpec = MaterialTheme.motionScheme.defaultEffectsSpec<Color>(), label = \"color\" ) Box( modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize().clickable( interactionSource = interactionSource, indication = null ) {} ) { Text( text = \"Hello\", modifier = Modifier.graphicsLayer { scaleX = scale scaleY = scale transformOrigin = TransformOrigin.Center } .align(Alignment.Center), style = LocalTextStyle.current.copy(color = color, textMotion = TextMotion.Animated) ) }"

            - text: At
            - link "Google I/O 2026":
              - /url: https://io.google/2026
            - text: ", we announced that"
            - link "Material Android is “all-in” on Compose":
              - /url: https://io.google/2026/explore/technical-session-30
            - text: ", alongside the official"
            - link "Android Compose-first announcement":
              - /url: https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/05/android-ui-development-is-compose-first.html
            - text: ", marking a new chapter in Android development."
          - paragraph:
            - text: Later in 2026, we’ll promote M3 Expressive experimental APIs, making
            - link "Material Compose":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3?_gl=1*1gllpir*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0Mzk2ODQkajU0JGwwJGgw
            - text: 1.5.0 stable. Additionally, we’ll be integrating the new
            - link "Styles API":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/styles?_gl=1*1gllpir*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0Mzk2ODQkajU0JGwwJGgw
            - text: for easier, more flexible customization, and have already integrated
            - link "Navigation3":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/layouts/adaptive/build-adaptive-navigation?_gl=1*1gfyy5b*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0Mzk2ODQkajU0JGwwJGgw
            - text: into the Material adaptive library.
          - paragraph:
            - text: To focus on Compose going forward,
            - link "Material Views 1.14.0":
              - /url: https://github.com/material-components/material-components-android/releases/tag/1.14.0
            - text: (MDC-Android) will be our final stable release for the Views library. There’s never been a better time to migrate to
            - link "Jetpack Compose":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/migrate/migrate-xml-views-to-jetpack-compose
            - text: .
          - paragraph
        - region:

        - region:

          - text: Copy link
          - heading "The final Material Views release" [level=2]
          - paragraph:
            - text: For years, Material Design has been on a journey to redefine how to build UI on Android. We’ve seen
            - link "Jetpack Compose":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/compose
            - text: grow from an ambitious idea into the engine behind the world’s most beautiful apps. As Android’s modern, declarative toolkit, it’s designed to simplify and accelerate UI development with less code and powerful native tools.
          - paragraph: While Compose continues to accelerate, our updates for Views have become more focused. For the last few years, we’ve been preparing for a fundamental shift in Android development.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - figure:
            - button "Pause Video": pause
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph:
            - text: "Earlier this month, we reached a major milestone: the stable release of"
            - link "Material Views 1.14.0":
              - /url: https://github.com/material-components/material-components-android/releases/tag/1.14.0
            - text: "(MDC-Android). This release officially brings Material 3 Expressive to the Views framework, as well as other improvements, unlocking more delightful experiences for Android makers:"
          - list:
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Expressive themes
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Expressive list component
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Emphasized type scale
            - listitem:
              - paragraph: Expressive styles for 11 existing components, like buttons, sliders, progress indicators, and more
          - paragraph:
            - text: With this release, the Material Views library is now entering
            - strong: maintenance mode
            - text: . It won’t get any new features, but will receive critical bug fixes.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Going Compose-first section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Going Compose-first" [level=2]
          - paragraph:
            - text: Moving forward, Material Android is transitioning to focus all feature development on the
            - link "Material Compose library":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3?_gl=1*wkss8e*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0NDAyMjUkajYwJGwwJGgw
            - text: .
          - paragraph:
            - text: Later in 2026, Material Android will release Compose 1.5.0, which will promote M3 experimental APIs to stable, including M3 Expressive. M3 Expressive APIs are like an expansion pack to M3; you can opt in to them to deliver more premium Android experiences. This includes Material 3 Expressive components, motion systems, and more from the Expressive update.
            - link "Read about M3 Expressive":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/blog/building-with-m3-expressive?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=IO26
          - paragraph:
            - text: For designers, the
            - link "Material 3 Figma Design Kit":
              - /url: https://www.figma.com/community/file/1035203688168086460/material-3-design-kit
            - text: and our
            - link "design guidelines":
              - /url: https://m3.material.io/
            - text: will continue to reflect the latest of what’s available in the Material Compose library.
        - region:
          - button "copy link to Styles API & adaptive navigation section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - heading "Styles API & adaptive navigation" [level=2]
          - paragraph:
            - text: We also announced the upcoming integration of Compose
            - link "Styles":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/styles?_gl=1*u33d9*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0NDA4NzUkajQzJGwwJGgw
            - text: and the recently-launched
            - link "Adaptive Navigation":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/layouts/adaptive/build-adaptive-navigation?_gl=1*1o80alu*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0NDA4ODAkajM4JGwwJGgw
            - text: update
            - link "with the new Navigation3 library":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/guide/navigation/navigation-3?_gl=1*1ka87s6*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0NDA5MDAkajE4JGwwJGgw
            - text: .
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link

          - paragraph:
            - text: The
            - link "Compose Styles API":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/styles?_gl=1*1ycph1f*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0NDA5MTkkajYwJGwwJGgw
            - text: on Android will make it easier than ever to customize Material components. This will improve overall app performance by skipping the composition phase during style updates and will simplify creating cohesive brand experiences. Integration is ongoing, so stay tuned!
        - region:
          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link

          - button "copy link to this section": link
          - text: Copy link
          - paragraph:
            - text: For a long time, building adaptive layouts for foldables, tablets, and desktops was complex, requiring makers to manage and switch between navigation frameworks throughout the app. To solve this, we’ve deeply integrated the Material Adaptive library with
            - link "Navigation3":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/guide/navigation/navigation-3?_gl=1*1qvzpce*_ga*NTY0NTY0OTE2LjE3NzkzMzg2Nzg.*_ga_QPQ2NRV856*czE3Nzk0Mzk2NzgkbzckZzEkdDE3Nzk0NDA5OTYkajYwJGwwJGgw
            - text: . Since the navigation library now understands the intent of your screens through metadata, it handles the heavy lifting for you, making implementation much more efficient.
            - link "Build adaptive UIs with Material components today":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/adaptive-apps
        - region:

          - paragraph:
            - text: We know how much you’ve built on Views, but there’s never been a better time to
            - link "migrate to Jetpack Compose":
              - /url: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/migrate/migrate-xml-views-to-jetpack-compose
            - text: . Get started by migrating your apps screen-by-screen with our
            - link "new migration Android skill":
              - /url: https://github.com/android/skills
            - text: ", which you can use with Android Studio, Android CLI, or any other AI tool."
          - paragraph: Stay tuned for more updates coming to Material Compose!
